chunks: And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from Ahmad ibn Abi Nasr, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man inclined towards prostration but did not know whether he had bowed or not. He said: 'He has bowed.'
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And if he left two prostrations from one rak'ah, he must repeat it in any case.

If he forgot one of them, then remembered it in the second rak'ah before bowing, he straightened himself, prostrated for it, then stood up and resumed recitation or glorification, if he was one who glorifies in the last two rak'ahs, as we have previously mentioned.
And if he did not remember it until he bowed in the second rak'ah, he made it up after the final salutation and performed the two prostrations of forgetfulness.

key_terms.أَ رَكَعَ أَمْ لَمْ يَرْكَعْ: Whether he bowed or did not bow

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a person is unsure whether they bowed in prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the principle of *al-istishab* (presumption of continuity) by ruling that inclination towards prostration suffices for the validity of *ruku'*, reflecting the Shia juristic preference for ease in doubt. It further delineates the precise procedural remedies for *sahw* (forgetfulness), distinguishing between immediate correction within the prayer structure and post-prayer compensation (*qada*) with *sajdat al-sahw*, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for maintaining ritual integrity amidst human error.
